title: The Resurrection of the Body
summary: The Church teaches that at the end of time, the same body each person now has will be reunited with their soul and raised to life, transformed and glorified — not merely that the soul survives, but that the whole human person, body and soul, will live forever.

blocks.text: An Article of the Creed From the Beginning

Christians have professed faith in the resurrection of the body since apostolic times. The Apostles' Creed uses the striking phrase 'resurrection of the flesh' (in Greek, sarkos anastasin), while the Creed drawn up at the Councils of Nicaea and Constantinople (325 and 381) speaks of 'the resurrection of the dead.' These are not two different beliefs — both affirm the same truth: that it is not just the soul that lives on, but that our actual bodies, the ones we have now, will one day be raised to new life.
For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth... then in my flesh I shall see God.

This hope did not appear suddenly with Christ. It grew gradually across the Old Testament — from a vague trust that God would not abandon the faithful to the grave, to the explicit hope voiced by the mother and her seven martyred sons in the Second Book of Maccabees, who accepted death confident that the Creator would give them back their bodies and their breath.
Christ's Own Resurrection Is the Foundation
But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have fallen asleep.

Everything the Church teaches about our own future resurrection rests on the fact that it already happened, definitively, in Christ. His Resurrection was not a resuscitation back to ordinary earthly life, nor a purely spiritual survival — his real body, the one that had been crucified, was raised, transformed, and glorified. Saint Paul calls this the 'first fruits': what happened to Christ's body is the pattern and the guarantee of what will happen to ours.

blocks.title: Council Definition / CCC Reference
blocks.text: The Fourth Lateran Council (1215), later reaffirmed at the Second Council of Lyons (1274), formally defined that all the dead will rise 'with their own bodies which they now bear' — decisively ruling out any interpretation of resurrection as merely spiritual or as involving a different body than the one a person actually had (cf. CCC 990, 1000).

Exactly how this happens lies beyond what reason or imagination can grasp; it is known only through faith. What can be said is that the body which rises is genuinely continuous with the body a person had in life, yet radically transformed — freed from weakness, corruption, and death itself. Christ's Transfiguration, in which his ordinary body was momentarily seen shining with divine glory, is often taken as a preview of what a glorified human body will be like.
I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live.

This resurrection is reserved for the end of time — 'the last day' — and concerns every person who has ever lived, not only the righteous. It is the necessary completion of the particular judgment each soul faces at death: body and soul, reunited, share together in the destiny the whole person has already begun to experience.

blocks.title: For the Faithful Departed
blocks.text: Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. May the souls of the faithful departed, through the mercy of God, rest in peace. Amen.
